svg.title: An MCP tool call routed from host to client to server and back, with what the harness still owns
svg.desc: A hand-drawn figure of one loop turn. On the left, the host, which is the harness: a MODEL box that runs the loop and decides when to call a tool, an MCP CLIENT box below it, one per server, speaking JSON-RPC over stdio or HTTP, and under both a panel recording what crosses at connect time, before step one: the host calls tools/list once and caches it, every returned schema is advertised to the model exactly like a local tool, and five typical servers come to about 55,000 tokens of definitions before any work is done. On the right, an MCP server running as a separate process, which owns and runs the tool, shown with two tools named search_docs and create_ticket, a note that the tool runs there and that its code and dependencies never enter yours, the JSON result that crosses back at step five, reading content, type text, text TICKET-4417 created, and a note that what the boundary buys is that the same server works with any host, so the model or the harness can be swapped and the ticket server is unchanged. Six numbered steps trace the call: one, the model emits a tool call; two, the host routes it to the client for that server; three, the client sends tools/call over the transport; four, the server runs the tool out of your process; five, the result returns over the same transport; and six, it becomes the model next observation. A bottom row gives the three runtime concerns the harness owns rather than the protocol. Validation: the result arrives over the wire as data, so a misbehaving server is untrusted input and its shape is validated before the model sees it. Failure: a timeout or a disconnect surfaces as an error saying the ticketing server is unavailable, never an exception that kills the loop. Injection surface: tool descriptions are attacker-controlled text that lands before any call, and in May 2025 a malicious public-repository issue leaked private repositories. A closing line records that the catalogue crosses at connect time and only the result crosses at step five.
svg.text: MCP dispatch inside one loop turn
The harness is the host; a client speaks MCP to a server that owns the tool. One turn, six steps.
HOST: THE HARNESS
MODEL
runs the loop and decides when to call a tool
MCP CLIENT
one per server; JSON-RPC over stdio or HTTP
AT CONNECT, BEFORE STEP 1: tools/list ONCE, THEN CACHED
Every returned schema is advertised to the model,
exactly like a local tool. Five typical servers:
about 55,000 tokens of definitions before any work.
MCP SERVER: A SEPARATE PROCESS
owns and runs the tool
search_docs
create_ticket
the tool runs here, in the server process
its code and dependencies never enter yours
WHAT CROSSES BACK, AT STEP 5
{"content": [{"type": "text",
"text": "TICKET-4417 created"}]}
SO THE BOUNDARY BUYS
the same server works with any host: swap the model
or the harness and the ticket server is unchanged.
stdio or HTTP
1 the model emits a tool call
2 the host routes it to the client for that server
3 the client sends tools/call over the transport
4 the server runs the tool, out of your process
5 the result returns over the same transport
6 and becomes the model next observation
VALIDATION
Check the result
The result arrives over the wire as data. A
misbehaving server is untrusted input:
validate the shape before the model sees it.
FAILURE
An observation, not a crash
A timeout or a disconnect surfaces as "error:
ticketing server unavailable", never an
exception that kills the loop.
INJECTION SURFACE
The schema arrives first
Tool descriptions are attacker-controlled
text that lands before any call. In May 2025
a public-repo issue leaked private ones.
One turn, six steps, two processes: the catalogue crosses at connect time, and only the result crosses at step 5.
